content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper proposes a variant of ensemble learning for deep networks, more specifically a multi-headed network trained by co-distillation. The authors propose some new defitions for ensemble loss, that is an ensembling loss and a co-distillation loss. The authors show that the proposed losses result in better performing ensembles, while not requiring more computational power.

I would vote for rejecting this paper. The paper suffers from an important experimental drawback, in that it does not compare the proposed methods with baselines from the state of the art (other than single models). The authors state themselves in the paper that the proposed losses are different from the losses in the co-distillation papers, which consist of a combination of the two losses. Without a proper comparison to the state of the art, it is impossible to say if the paper provides a significant contribution or not. 

Furthermore, the methodological contributions appear to be rather incremental. In order to be publishable, they would need be justified by significant experimental proof, which is currently lacking.

Section 4, paragraph 1, what does "about three runs" mean? It's either 3 runs or it's not three runs. If results are computed on more or less than three runs, it should be explicited.

In short, I would say that the paper is well written and presented, but I think it is also rather incremental and lacks more baselines to warrant a publication at ICLR or a similar conference.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful review.

The baseline models in the paper such as Resnet/SE-Resnet are widely used strong models. We had many theoretical and experimental comparisons and showed a simple distillation offers good enhancement across a variety of datasets with tuning a single hyperparameter $\mu$. Many state-of-the-art models are achieved by heavily tuning dozens of hyperparameters on specific domains, and they have very limited transferability. (eg, they are not quite usable as production models to solve real problems by tech companies)

Besides, we also compared our delta improvement with those of similar approaches from other papers at the end of page 4.

Can you be more specific on what comparisons you would like to see?

content.title: more details
content.comment:
Let me phrase my complaints differently. You present a method to train multi-headed networks, propose some theory to link it to what is dubbed 'ensembling' and to co-distillation. Why should people reading your paper care about the proposed method, rather than just going for a previously published multi-headed ensemble approach? Single model approaches do not constitute "ensembling baselines" as they consist of single models and it is already widely known that ensemble methods outperform single models. This leaves us with comparisons to other ensembling methods, which are very limited in the paper. The performance of (Lan et al., 2018) and (Wang et al., 2018) is cited in the section on ImageNet classification, but it is hard to know if they had the same exact structure for splitting the network head, and hence it is hard to know if the comparison is valid. You suggested elsewhere that making network heads larger or smaller without changing their number would likely impact their performance, perhaps something similar is at play here, however there is no way to tell. More detail on this is needed, and if there is a fit between the methods, they should be added to Table 1. I would suggest to rerun the same exact network structure with the different loss functions proposed in those papers (such as the hybrid loss proposed in the codistillation paper by Anil et al., 2018). 

If we assume the comparisons on ImageNet are valid, on the other two benchmarks we are still left with only one point of comparison as there are no "ensembling" baselines. Again, in my opinion this doesn't bring any new information to a prospective reader, given that the cited work already proved the viability of co-distillation for single pass multi-headed deep network training.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Here is the new information we bring.

1. People have been using the traditional simple average ensembling widely but don't realize that they can improve the performance by decreasing $\lambda$ to a negative value. Even if they do play with the ensembling loss, they don't realize that it's theoretically similar to the co-distillation loss. There is no evidence in favor of mixing the two. We can add more experiments to support it, but none of the cited papers even answers the question whether co-distillation is better than simple average ensembling (which is a strong baseline) or not.

2. We reduce head sizes and use all of the heads in inference. This is different from cited works, but that's part of our contribution. At the end of the day, the cited works and our work all compare with the respective single models. If anyone can get easy wins by using our approach, why not do it? It's natural that one should consider the sizes of the branches. People don't realize that they can easily improve model performance by >2% if they do this.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
The authors proposed a new approach for the end-to-end training of ensembles of neural networks. The method consists of two steps. The first one is the construction of a multi-head architecture from a base neural network. The second step is training this model using a co-distillation loss function, where different heads are treated as elements of an ensemble.
The idea behind EnsembleNet is similar to the multi-head architecture, but instead of just simply multiply upper blocks to obtain several heads, the authors also proposed to shrink these heads. This idea is not significantly different from multi-head model. Also, the authors noticed that the proposed approach almost does not benefit from more than two heads..


Experimental results are quite promising and quite broad in terms of the number of problems to which this method was applied. Nevertheless, it would be beneficial to compare the proposed method with other memory efficient techniques such as: e.g. Shake-Shake regularization [1], deep mutual learning approach [2] in which according the table 2 the co-distillation of two models help to boost the performance of each of them and other similar approaches.
[1]  Gastaldi, Xavier. "Shake-shake regularization." arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.07485 (2017).
[2]  Ying  Zhang,  Tao  Xiang,  Timothy  M  Hospedales,  and  Huchuan  Lu.   Deep  mutual  learning.   In Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition,  pp. 4320–4328, 2018

Overall, the paper is interesting but the ideas on which it is based are quite simple and not quite new. The experimental part is promising but should include comparison with other similar approaches. Another concern is scalability of this approach to more than two heads.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful review.

Performance on large scale datasets such ImageNet is much more convincing and reliable than that on small scale ones such as Cifar. The two papers you referred to don't have results on ImageNet. There are similar papers that did report metrics on ImageNet, and we did do comparisons with them at the end of page 4.

By keeping total model sizes the same, we didn’t observe additional gains by going for more than 2 or 3 heads. It’s not really a concern. It’s just there is no need to go for more. By the way, if we keep each head the same and increase the number of heads, the performance does keep going up, but this is at the cost of increased total model sizes.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
I would like to thank the authors for their answers.
 
You are absolutely right that experimental results on ImageNet are more convincing than results on small datasets in most of the cases. Nevertheless, the referred papers potentially can be applied to ImageNet and may deliver similar results to the method described in the paper. I believe there should be added a comparison with more approaches at least on small datasets since the provided approach is quite simple and significantly overlaps with many methods in terms of the domain of their applicability.

“By the way, if we keep each head the same and increase the number of heads, the performance does keep going up, but this is at the cost of increased total model sizes.” Yes, it partially alleviates my concern, but I would like to know how the accuracy grows with respect to the number of heads.

Based on the authors’ replies I would like to slightly increase my score. I still believe that the idea is quite simple and this is an incremental work.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper presents "EnsembleNet" a multihead neural network architecture where the multiple heads have the same architecture and are all (roughly) trying to predict the same thing.  The diversity of this "ensemble" comes from the random weight initialization.  The paper investigates and compares the ensemble loss structure and the co-distillation loss structure.  They make the interesting observation that for the ensembling loss structure, performance is better when one puts a negative weight on the loss of the ensemble (the mean of the multiple heads) while putting larger weights on the performance of the individual head losses. They also show that for the case of square loss, if the ensembling model is a simple average, then the ensembling loss and the co-distillation loss are equivalent. Finally, they present a general strategy for converting a network to an EnsembleNet.

They hyperparameter tune with both losses and find that the co-distillation loss is marginally better than the ensemble loss structure.  Overall gains over baseline seem moderate.  

I don't think this paper is an accept.  It has a couple interesting insights, but they seem rather subtle... perhaps this would be of interest to people who are specifically researching these types of ensembles.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful review.

Ensembling is a universally useful tool for boosting model performance. Please refer to top entries in most Kaggle competitions. We offer both theoretical and experimental evidence on how to ensemble models in general. Anyone who uses ensembling, or even anyone who trains machine learning models may want to consider our approach.
